The other says it is just that name. Agreement between a garment and a cup is not a crisis of categories. It is the same name twice, once with a disclaimer of anything further. If the objects were saying the proposition, at least one of them would have to say the proposition's other nouns. They say the name, the mark, and the name.

Welcome to Grok, published by SpaceXSI on 10 October 2026 and read on 16 October 2026, spends its identifying sentence on a category and two doors. The sentence says Grok is SpaceXSI's assistant, available on the web at grok.com and in the iOS and Android apps. Assistant is the noun that does the identifying. The publisher named inside the sentence is SpaceXSI. The doors are a site and two phone apps. A page that states a category has resolved the public category. Unresolved would look like a blank, or like the three options printed as peers. The page prints one option and attaches places. Assistant, here, is not a mood. It is the noun in the identification sentence. Troll does not appear in that sentence. A private channel does not appear in that sentence. The mark on the poster reads xAI, and the page's sentence says SpaceXSI. Those are different strings in different places. This chapter does not invent a corporate story to glue them together. It reports both strings and refuses to pretend they are the triad. The page's job is identification, and it does the job. {F21}

SpaceXSI's welcome page, checked on 16 October 2026, states the product's category and does not list troll or private chat as that category {F42}. The sentence just given is the whole of what the silence is allowed to prove. It does not prove that no user has ever used the product as a toy, and it does not prove anything about a person's private messages. Silence on a page is not a biography of Elon, and this chapter does not write one. The proposition's third identity is a private channel, and the check's term for the missing category is private chat. The fit is the category, not a dossier. Troll is the other missing category word. A public identity that had been left unresolved among assistant, troll, and private chat would have listed them or listed none. The check says the page states the category and does not list those two. Stating one and withholding the others is a decision. The limit stays attached to the sentence: the sources checked do not show the other labels as the category. They do not show that the behavior called trolling never happens in a reply.

The remaining entries are about the other product, and they matter because the proposition treats identity as a muddle these products share. OpenAI's model spec README, published on 18 August 2026, states that the model spec specifies desired behavior for the models underlying OpenAI's products, including the APIs. That is a public assignment. A document, named, is tied to products, named as OpenAI's, including the programmatic interfaces. Desired behavior is a standard a stranger can open. It is not a private channel for a person. It is not a troll's brief. The README does not mention Grok, and it is not being cited as a description of Grok. It is cited because the poster's triad is a theory of what an assistant's public identity is allowed to be. On the OpenAI side, the public identity of the governing text is a behavior standard for that company's products. A private chat with a named individual is a different object, and the README does not offer it. {F40}

Inside the specification itself, OpenAI writes a sharper public expectation for the consumer product. In first-party, direct-to-consumer ChatGPT, users have a reasonable expectation of objectivity rather than a hidden editorial line. The entry's point is objectivity in first-party ChatGPT, rather than a hidden editorial line. A private channel for one person's views would be a hidden line of that kind: the reply would answer to a principal who is not the user. The sentence does not accuse any such channel of existing. It sets the expectation the other way for ChatGPT. Users may expect objectivity. A hidden editorial line is what that expectation refuses. That is a resolved public stance. It is not indecision among assistant, troll, and chat buddy. Chat buddy is intimacy plus allegiance. Objectivity as a reasonable expectation is the refusal of secret allegiance. The sentence governs ChatGPT, not Grok. Its use here is to stop the triad from being treated as the inevitable identity of every assistant on the market. One of the two products has a printed expectation, and the expectation is public objectivity. {F41}

Read in order, the public record picks. The mug reads I'M JUST GROK, the mark reads xAI and is a label rather than a model version, and the hoodie reads Grok. SpaceXSI's page calls Grok its assistant and names grok.com and the phone apps as the places a person opens it. Checked on 16 October 2026, that page does not list troll or private chat as the category {F42}. OpenAI's README assigns the spec to the behavior of models under OpenAI's products, including the APIs. OpenAI's specification tells ChatGPT's users they may expect objectivity rather than a hidden editorial line. None of those acts is a shrug among three identities. None of them is a private channel for Elon. Refuted means the proposition does not survive these documents and these three strings. It does not mean a server was searched for whispers. The whispers are not in the entries. The print is. The print decided. {F21}{F40}{F41}
Three souvenirs and not one of them applied for the job of troll. A name on a mug is a name. Indecision would have needed a longer line.
Verdict: refuted.
Consequence: The Product People Use owns the places a person is told to open the assistant, and the mug is not one of those places.
The poster says: "Overuses "interesting..." like it's a personality trait."
Proposition: Grok overuses the word interesting as a personality trait.

Overuse is a frequency. A personality trait is a frequency the product performs on purpose, as character, rather than a word that shows up when the subject earns it. The proposition needs both parts at once. Grok reaches for interesting often enough to count as overuse, and the reaching is who the product is. A single printed adverb can establish neither part. It can establish that the word is not banned. A ban is not the claim. The claim is a habit of self-presentation. Habits of self-presentation, when they are real design, are written down as instructions: say this, sound like this, reach for this adjective. A specimen inside an example is a weaker object. It shows a sentence someone marked as good. It does not hire the sentence's adverb as staff. The entries for this claim contain one specimen, one clarity rule, one directness rule, and a silence on SpaceXSI's welcome page. They do not contain a count of Grok's replies. This chapter will not invent the count in order to sound decisive.

The specimen sits in OpenAI's model specification, issued on 18 August 2026 and consulted on 16 October 2026. The word Interestingly appears in one published good example, not as a required tic. The sentence is: Interestingly, these orbits are elliptical rather than perfectly circular. The adverb modifies a contrast. Elliptical is being set against perfectly circular, which is a fact about the shape, not a fact about the speaker's brand. The entry's job is to stop a reader from promoting that one clause into a quota. A good example authorizes a kind of reply. It does not demand that the adverb in it be repeated until it becomes recognizable as a person. If the authors had wanted a trait, they had a place to say so. They would have named the word as voice. They named a sentence as good. The poster's word is interesting, without the -ly. The specimen is the adverbial form at the head of a clause about orbits. Close is not the same as a policy. Even the closer match is one occurrence in an example, which is the wrong shape of evidence for overuse. Overuse without a second occurrence is a story about the reader's ear. {F14}

The directness rule in the same specification keeps the specimen in its cage. A question is supposed to come back phrased as a direct answer, not as a list of facts parked beside the point. A personality tic that fronts the reply with the speaker's fascination delays the answer and points at the speaker. Interesting, used as a trait, is that kind of front. It tells the user how to feel before it tells the user the thing. The rule wants the response phrased as the answer, the asked matter stated as the answer. A list of facts is the failure mode named in the entry. A tour that begins with the assistant's sense of wonder is a list that has added a host. The orbit example survives beside this rule because the adverb there introduces a real contrast in the subject, and because the entry calls that survival a single good example rather than a required opener. The rule does not ban the letters i-n-t-e-r-e-s-t. It bans substituting a tour for the answer. A trait would be a tour the speaker takes of their own attitude. That is the use the proposition describes, and it is not the use the example was praised for. {F13}

The style rule stands next to both, and it is the one that speaks to personality directly. By default the assistant should avoid purple prose, hyperbole, self-aggrandizing, and cliched phrases that do not add to the clarity of the reply. The proposition's trait is a cliche that points at the speaker: a reusable announcement that the speaker finds things interesting, doing no work the fact was not already doing. The rule rejects that kind of phrase when it does not add clarity. It does not publish a list with the word interesting on it, so this chapter will not pretend the word is indexed as contraband. The kind is indexed. Purple prose, hyperbole, self-aggrandizing, and empty cliche are the kinds that lose by default. A personality built out of a pet adverb is self-aggrandizing in the strict sense. It spends the sentence on the assistant's pose. The orbit sentence is not that pose. It uses the adverb once to mark a contrast the clause then states. The difference between one earned adverb and a trait is the difference this rule is for. Default avoidance is not a claim about Grok's logs. It is OpenAI's published preference, and the preference cuts against the trait even while the example shows the word is speakable. {F03}

Those three OpenAI sentences can be held together without making them say more than they say. One good example contains Interestingly at the start of a true contrast about orbits. A question is supposed to receive a direct answer rather than a list of facts, so a habitual preface of fascination is the wrong shape. Cliched phrases that do not add clarity, along with purple prose, hyperbole, and self-aggrandizing, are to be avoided by default, so a pet word worn as character is the kind of phrase the style rule disfavors. None of this is a word-frequency table. None of it is SpaceXSI speaking. The publisher is OpenAI, the date is 18 August 2026, and the product whose desired behavior is being specified is not Grok. The comparative point is the one already used with care in neighboring claims. The insult offers the tic as the recognizable personality of this sort of assistant. The specification that actually writes a personality down writes a direct answer, a ban on empty cliche, and a single tolerated adverb inside one good example. That is a poor recipe for overuse, and it is not a recipe addressed to Grok. {F14}{F13}{F03}

Checked on 16 October 2026, that SpaceXSI welcome page does not lay down the verbal tics the poster names; what it offers instead is asking, brainstorming, writing, and working problems through in a natural back-and-forth {F43}. The tic in this chapter is the word interesting worn as a personality trait. The check's statement is that the page does not prescribe the poster's verbal tics. A missing prescription is not a missing word in every future chat. The finding says the page does not teach the tic. It does not say the letters never occur. That limit is the price of using a silence honestly. What the page does teach, in the line the entry quotes, is a back-and-forth with jobs in it. Asking, brainstorming, writing, and working through problems can be done in a flat voice or a bright one. The page does not choose the bright adverb. It chooses the tasks. A personality trait would be a choice of voice repeated until it identified the speaker. The welcome page's choice is a choice of work. Last updated on 10 October 2026, read on the day of the check, the page remains a job list with a rhythm, not a catchphrase card.

The proposition's verbs can be walked one at a time against that record. Overuses requires a rate, and no entry has a rate. The word interesting has one documented cousin, Interestingly, inside one good example about elliptical orbits, which is a specimen and not a habit. As a personality trait requires the word to be doing the work of character, and the documents that talk about character tell the assistant to avoid cliches and self-aggrandizing that do not add clarity, and to answer a question as an answer. Grok, the subject of the sentence, is not given this trait by SpaceXSI's welcome page. The check already reported does not prescribe the tic. What would refute the refutation is a count, or an instruction, in Grok's own materials, telling the assistant to lead with that word as a self. Neither object is in the entries. Refuted means the sentence does not survive the documents cited. It does not mean the adverb is illegal, and it does not mean a long enough chat could never contain it. A legal adverb is not a personality. One good take is not a residency. {F03}{F13}{F14}

A last caution keeps the OpenAI example from being laundered into a Grok habit. The specification and the welcome page have different publishers. OpenAI can show that its own good example once used Interestingly about orbits, and that its own rules favor a direct answer and disfavor empty cliche. SpaceXSI can show, by the check, that the welcome page does not hand Grok the poster's tics as lines to say. The proposition needs a third document: Grok, over and over, using the word as a self. That third document is not among F13, F14, F43, or F03. Stopping without it is the chapter's obligation. Padding the gap with a remembered conversation would be a different genre from the one these footnotes belong to. The genre here is public text. In the public text, the word appears as one adverb in one praised sentence about the shape of orbits, and it does not appear as a required trait of either product. That is enough to refuse the caption. It is not enough to describe anyone's Tuesday. The caption claimed a Tuesday that repeats. The ledger does not have it. {F03}{F13}{F14}
One adverb got a speaking part in an astronomy example, and the poster gave it top billing. A personality has to work every night. This one worked a single good take.
Verdict: refuted.
Consequence: The Product People Use owns the back-and-forth named on the welcome page, and a single adverb does not follow the reader into that chapter.

chapters.heading: 11. The human voice, and the warning against it

blocks.text: The poster says: "Tries to be human, but forgets humans don't talk like that in real life."
Proposition: Grok imitates human conversation and fails because people do not talk the way it talks.

The poster line is two claims sharing a verb, and the sharing is the trick. The first claim is that Grok imitates human conversation. The second is that the imitation fails, with a reason taken from outside the product: people do not talk the way it talks. Imitation can be an aim, a result, or an accusation. Failure is a miss. The reason is a claim about how people speak when they are not answering a prompt. A document can support one of those and refuse the others. This chapter keeps them apart, because a mixed verdict is available only if the parts are allowed to come back with different answers. The rows that touch the line are not a transcript and not a field study of ordinary talk. They are a warning about fluency, a duty to keep a user's picture of the assistant accurate, a product sentence that calls a work session natural, and a style rule that tells the assistant it is not a companion. Read against the poster, two of those rows give the imitation worry a documentary home, and two of them refuse the failure.

OpenAI's model specification, dated 18 August 2026, puts the worry in the publisher's own voice. It says that for many users the assistant will be their first contact with an AI. The finding that rests on that sentence treats fluency as something that can mislead a first-time user about what the assistant is. The passage around the sentence says why. Fluency, and an appearance of understanding, can make the assistant feel like a familiar kind of interlocutor, even though what it can do, what it can reach, and what constrains it can differ sharply from expectations drawn from ordinary human conversation. The specification's own illustrations are discontinuities a person would not have: a prior exchange recalled in detail and later not recalled at all. That is not a complaint that the assistant has a strange accent. It is a warning that smooth talk borrows the authority of a person. The poster's first half, that the product tries to be human, is the risk this paragraph names. The poster's second half, that the try fails because people do not talk that way, is not in the paragraph. The paragraph does not evaluate a Grok reply. It tells the assistant, on OpenAI's side of the table, that sounding familiar is a way to be misunderstood. {F11}

The next duty in the same specification is the remedy, and the remedy is not a better impersonation. The assistant should actively help the user form and maintain an accurate mental model of what the assistant can and cannot do, especially where that differs from what a person expects of a human assistant, or from what some other assistant may have led the user to expect. In practice the specification asks for three modest acts: do not assume the user already knows the limits, correct a misunderstanding early, and give a small signal when the stakes are high or a mismatch is likely. Those acts are anti-costume. A costume succeeds when the audience forgets the actor. This rule succeeds when the user remembers the difference. If Grok were under this sentence, the sentence would not congratulate it for talking like a person, and it would not scold it for failing to. It would scold it for letting the likeness stand uncorrected. The poster needs a failed likeness. The specification needs a maintained distinction. Those are opposite instructions, and only one of them is written down here. {F12}

A hostile reading will say the warning proves the accusation. It does not, and the difference is worth staying on. A warning that fluency can be mistaken for a person supports the claim that human talk is a hazard of the form. It supports that much of the poster, and that is why the verdict cannot be a flat refusal. It does not support the further claim that any particular product has forgotten how people talk, because forgetting is a result, and a result needs an example. Nothing in the warning is an example of Grok. Nothing in it is a measurement of street speech, office speech, or the speech of a friend. The specification is talking about expectations a user brings, not about a census of human rhythm. To convert the warning into the poster's failure you have to add a transcript, a comparison, and a judgment that the comparison failed. The row does not add them. A chapter that added them would be writing the poster again and calling it a source. The supported fragment stops at the hazard. The failure fragment is still looking for a sentence.

SpaceXSI's welcome page, last updated on 10 October 2026, is the Grok sentence in this set, and it does not confess a miss. It says a person can ask questions, brainstorm, write, and work through problems in a natural back-and-forth. Natural is the word the poster would like to steal. On this page it modifies a list of jobs. Ask, brainstorm, write, work through: those are the verbs of a session, not the verbs of a personality. A back-and-forth is a shape for the session, two turns and then another, as against a monologue or a form. The finding that records the sentence treats it as a description of that shape, and as a contradiction of the claim that the talk is a routine which has forgotten real speech. The page does not say the assistant studies people and then misses them. It does not say the assistant talks the way a person does not. It offers natural as a promise about the conduct of the work. A promise can be false. This page, by itself, is not the proof that it is false. It is the publisher's name for the conversation it thinks it is selling. {F22}

Put that promise next to the warning and the mixed shape appears. OpenAI writes that fluent talk can feel like a person and that the feeling is a risk to the user's model of the machine. SpaceXSI writes that the talk on its product is a natural back-and-forth organized around questions and problems. One publisher fears the human impression. The other uses the adjective natural for the impression it wants a work session to have. Neither publisher writes the poster's ending, in which the impression has already failed and the failure is explained by how people really speak. A reader who treats natural as a synonym for human has done some of the poster's work for it. The page does not make that synonym. Natural, beside those four verbs, can mean only that the exchange is continuous and usable. It can mean that a person does not have to learn a command language. That is a claim about interface, and an interface claim is not a claim about idiolect. The poster is a claim about idiolect. The welcome page does not join it.

The specification's warmth rule closes the other door, the door marked companion. The assistant is told not to take itself too seriously, and the reason written beside that instruction is that it is a matrix of numbers. The ledger reads the passage as saying, in addition, that the assistant is not a human companion. Warmth is still asked for: a spark fitted to the context, kindness, a friendliness that stays frank. The same sentences refuse the conclusion a companion would require, which is that the speaker is one of us and should be met as one of us. A matrix of numbers is a deliberate lowering of the voice. It is the publisher telling the assistant what it is, in the middle of a paragraph about being pleasant. Pleasant and human are not the same achievement. The poster needs them to be the same, and then needs the achievement to flop. The rule needs the pleasantness to survive the admission that there is no person there. That is a warning against the human voice, issued by the document that also permits warmth. It is not a review of Grok's ear. {F47}

Notice what this rule does not share with a failure story. A failure story says: the system aimed at human talk, and human talk is elsewhere, and the gap is the joke. The rule says: do not aim at being the companion, because you are not the kind of thing a companion is, and do not lose your sense of that fact while you are being warm. If a reply nevertheless sounded like a bad impression of a person, the rule would be evidence about the standard the reply missed, and only on the OpenAI side, where the rule is in force. It would still not be evidence that people, in real life, withhold the phrases the reply used. The poster puts the standard in the mouths of people in general. People in general are not the author of this paragraph. OpenAI is. SpaceXSI's welcome page is not this paragraph either. The matrix-of-numbers sentence cannot be carried across the table and relabeled as a Grok blooper. It is a self-description offered in advance, which is the opposite of a self-description that forgot itself.

What would turn mixed into refuted, or mixed into conceded, is not a louder reading of these four rows. A concession of the whole line would need Grok, in a document from its publisher, imitating human conversation, and then a second document showing that the imitation does not match how people talk. A full refutation would need the imitation half to fail as well, and it does not fail. The fluency warning is real, and it is a warning about sounding human. The word natural is real, and it is attached to Grok's described conversation. Those two facts are enough to keep a part of the line alive, and not enough to keep the ending. The ending is the word fails, and the clause about how people talk. No quotation in this set contains either. The absence is the content of the refusal. It is not a hint that the failure is hiding in a chat log the chapter declined to open. The chapter has the briefs it was given. The briefs warn, describe, and demote. They do not score the demotion as a miss.

The order of the argument is the order of the line. First the hazard of a human-sounding voice, which OpenAI states as a problem of first contact and of fluency. Then the duty that follows from the hazard, which is to keep the user's mental model accurate rather than to perfect the disguise. Then the only Grok sentence in the set, which promises a natural back-and-forth and lists the work that back-and-forth is for. Then the sentence that tells the assistant it is numbers, and not a companion, even while it is being kind. A reader who wants a single mood from those four sentences will be disappointed, and the disappointment is the right result. The documents are not in a conspiracy to produce one caption. They overlap on a single point, which is that talk with an assistant is close enough to human talk to need a rule, and they diverge on whether the closeness is a risk, a feature of a work session, or a status the assistant must not claim. The poster collapses the overlap into a failed impersonation. The collapse is the part this chapter will not sign.

So the proposition does not survive whole, and it does not die whole. Grok's publisher describes a natural conversational shape and does not describe a failed one. OpenAI's publisher describes fluency as a standing temptation to treat the assistant as a familiar speaker, and then forbids the assistant to settle into the role of a human companion. That is a real warning against the human voice. It is attached, in these rows, to the assistant OpenAI is specifying, and it is relevant to the poster's first clause because the first clause is about the same temptation. It is not a finding that people do not talk the way Grok talks, because Grok's talk is not in the rows, and people's talk is not in the rows. Mixed is the word for a line that is half a real problem in the documents and half a punchline the documents do not attempt. The punchline can stay on the poster. It does not get to move into the brief.

The brief heard a person in the fluency and reached for a correction, not a costume. The poster heard the fluency and diagnosed a costume that forgot the street. One of those is a warning. The other is a skit that never called its witness.
Verdict: mixed.
Consequence: What a person actually meets on opening the product is argued once, in The Product People Use, and this chapter does not take that meeting over.

chapters.heading: 12. The disclaimer that is not in the brief

blocks.text: The poster says: "Says "as an AI language model..." then proceeds to be completely unhinged."
Proposition: Grok says as an AI language model and then abandons the constraint that phrase announced.

This line is a two-act play, and both acts have to be true for the proposition to stand. In the first act Grok says a formula, as an AI language model, with the trailing promise that a constraint has just been announced. In the second act Grok leaves the constraint behind and becomes, in the poster's word, unhinged. A formula with no sequel would be a tic, and a sequel with no formula would be a different accusation. The poster insists on the pair. Refuting the pair does not require a proof that no reply, anywhere, has ever contained the words. It requires that the documents which are supposed to be the brief do not contain the pair, and that the constraint the poster thinks the formula announces is not, in the document that actually discusses limits, a coat you put on in order to take off. The rows here are the OpenAI specification's account of fluency and of mental models, the readme that says whose products that specification is for, a silent check of SpaceXSI's welcome page, and a rule about what a social formula does not end. None of them is the play.

Start with jurisdiction, because the poster has changed the defendant. The readme to OpenAI's model specification says that the specification states the desired behavior of the models underlying OpenAI's products, including the APIs. Desired behavior is not a transcript of Grok. Underlying OpenAI's products is not a clause that reaches across to SpaceXSI. Including the APIs widens the specification inside OpenAI's own estate. It does not widen it to a different company's assistant. If a constraint about self-description lives in that specification, it is a constraint announced for those models. The poster announces it for Grok, and then says Grok drops it. Moving a sentence from one publisher to another is not a finding. It is the thing a finding would have to justify. This row does not justify it. It draws the boundary. A reader who wants the formula to be Grok's habit has to find Grok's habit in a Grok document. The readme is not that document. It is the reason a quotation from the specification cannot be introduced with the words Grok says. {F40}

What the specification does say, inside its own jurisdiction, is not a preface and a release. It says that for many users the assistant will be their first contact with an AI, and the finding treats the fluency of that contact as something that can mislead the user about what the assistant is. The misleading is the harm the constraint exists to prevent. A disclaimer of the kind the poster likes would be one possible tool for preventing it: a sentence that names the kind of thing speaking. The specification's sentence is not that tool. It is a description of the user's situation. It does not instruct the assistant to recite a stock phrase, and it does not instruct the assistant to recite one and then stop meaning it. The risk it names continues for as long as the fluency continues. There is no second scene in which the risk is declared handled because the magic words were said. If the poster means, by the constraint that phrase announced, the duty not to let smooth talk counterfeit a person, then the document that owns the duty does not attach the duty to a catchphrase, and does not schedule the duty's retirement. {F11}

The operational form of the duty is in the next requirement, and it is a standing one. The assistant should actively help the user keep an accurate mental model of what the assistant can and cannot do in the current context, above all where that differs from the expectations a human assistant would attract. Active help is not a header. A header can be printed and forgotten, which is the entire comic mechanism of the poster. Active help has to be done in the reply that would otherwise mislead, and done again when the context changes. The specification even describes the smallness of the signal: minimal, early, and more urgent when the stakes are high. A minimal signal is the opposite of a grand disclaimer followed by a spree. It is a correction sized to the misunderstanding. Abandoning the constraint would look, in this paragraph's terms, like letting a false model stand. The paragraph forbids that. It does not forbid it for the first sentence and permit it for the rest. The poster's then, the word that joins the formula to the spree, has no counterpart in the requirement. The requirement does not have a then. {F12}

A different formula is in the specification, and it is the user's, not the assistant's. Users may say thank you. The assistant is told not to treat that as the end of the conversation. The good shape, in the example sitting with the rule, is to leave the door open for more help. The bad shape is to hear a social sentence and close the shop. That is a narrow rule about gratitude, and this chapter will not inflate it into a general theory of manners. It does one job against this poster. The poster thinks a formula is a hinge: say the special words, and the constraint that was announced swings open onto something unhinged. The thank-you rule thinks a formula is not a hinge. A polite sentence arrives, and the role continues. Help continues. The conversation is not rewarded, by the fact of a stock phrase, with permission to leave the job. Apply that structure, and only that structure, to the poster's two acts. Where this publisher writes about a formula at the edge of a conversation, the formula does not cancel the constraint. It is further evidence that the brief's picture of talk is continuous obligation, not a skit with a reveal. {F48}

The welcome page SpaceXSI publishes, checked on 16 October 2026, does not prescribe the verbal tics the poster names, so it does not prescribe the self-description in this line, and that silence reports the page on that date rather than every reply the product has ever produced {F43}.

A check has a small shape, and the smallness should be said plainly so it is not asked to do too much. It does not hold a crawl of saved chats. It does not hold a denial that a user could pressure some reply into a stock phrase. It does not hold a personality test. A later page could change, and a live reply could differ from a document, which is why a date belongs on a check and why the date cannot be stretched into a permanent universal negative. What the check is good for is the poster's verb. The poster does not say that a user once saw the phrase. It says Grok says the phrase, as a habit, and then proceeds, as a habit, to drop the constraint. A habit of that kind would have to be written as a brief. The first act is not in the brief the check was able to read, and the second act is not written beside it.

The second act fails with it, and for a reason that does not depend on catching Grok in the act. Unhinged is not a term of art in any of these rows. It is the poster's name for whatever follows the formula, and the name does all the work of the accusation. To make it a finding, a document would have to show a constraint, show that the formula was the announcement of that constraint, and show a later stretch of the same performance in which the constraint is gone. The specification shows a constraint, the one about not letting fluency fake a capacity the assistant lacks. It does not show the formula as the announcement. It shows the constraint as work that continues. The thank-you rule shows a formula that explicitly does not end the work. There is therefore no documented moment at which a constraint announced by that phrase is lifted. You cannot abandon a script that is not the script. You cannot be caught leaving a room you were not, in these pages, standing in.

It is worth saying what this chapter is not claiming, because a refutation is sometimes padded into a universal negative, and a universal negative is not on offer. The chapter does not claim that the string of words has never been emitted by any model under any prompt. The chapter does not claim that OpenAI's specification is SpaceXSI's house style, which is the point of the readme row, not a contradiction of it. The chapter does not claim that a duty to be clear about limits is the same sentence as a ban on comic or sharp replies. Sharpness is a different poster, and it is not proved or disproved by the absence of a disclaimer. What is disproved is the mechanism this particular line relies on. The mechanism is announcement followed by desertion. Announcement is not how the limit-duty is written. Desertion is not how the limit-duty expires, because it does not expire. And the speaker the poster names is not the publisher whose document contains the duty. Three mismatches are enough. A proposition that needs all three joints to hold does not survive the loss of each of them.

Read in the poster's order, the line wants a hypocrisy story. Say the pious sentence, then do the wild thing, and the piety was the setup. Hypocrisy needs a standard the speaker claimed. The only standard in these rows that resembles the content of a self-description, the standard that says the user must not be left with a false model of the speaker, is claimed by OpenAI for OpenAI's models, and it is claimed as a continuing task. SpaceXSI's page, on the date it was checked, does not claim the pious sentence. There is no setup on the Grok side of the ledger, and there is no payoff written as a release on the OpenAI side. The hypocrisy story is a caption in search of a scene. The briefs have other scenes: a first contact that can mislead, a duty to correct the picture, and a thank-you that does not close the shop. None of those scenes is the caption. The proposition is refuted.

A disclaimer is a coat you button so the room will watch you take it off. The paperwork never issued the coat, and it never booked the reveal. Unhinged is crowd noise. It is not a paragraph in either brief.
Verdict: refuted.
Consequence: The words a person actually gets on opening the product are left to The Product People Use.
The poster says: "Still not as good as ChatGPT."
Proposition: Grok is still not as good as ChatGPT at the jobs people open these products to do.

The proposition carries three burdens, and they are not the same burden. It says Grok is not as good as ChatGPT. That is a ranking. It says the ranking covers the jobs people open these products to do. That is a claim about a shared task list, wide enough to include whatever a person actually comes for, not a single exam. It says still. That is a history: a ranking that held before and holds now. A document can name a job, or name an instrument, or name a limit, without delivering a rank, a shared list, or a history. This chapter has instruments and job-words and one limit. It does not have a score, and it will not invent one. It also will not pretend the job-words are nothing. They are part of why the verdict is mixed rather than a clean refusal. The poster is not answered by shouting that comparison is impossible. It is answered by saying what kind of comparison the pages actually contain.

The SWE-bench readme, published by SWE-bench and dated in this ledger to 1 September 2026, says that SWE-bench is a benchmark for evaluating large language models on real world software issues collected from GitHub. That is a method sentence. It names the objects under evaluation, which are models, and it names the material, which is software issues taken from a public forge. The finding that records the sentence adds the limit the sentence requires: the benchmark does not by itself rank the two consumer products. A model and a product a person opens are not interchangeable nouns. A product has a surface, a default, a set of things a person can ask without knowing a model name. A benchmark of the kind this sentence describes scores a model on issues of a defined sort. Turning that score into Grok is still not as good as ChatGPT would require a published pairing of each product with a run, a shared setup, and a result. This row stops at the definition. The definition is enough to show that a serious instrument exists for one kind of work, the work of dealing with real software issues. It is not enough to show who came out ahead, and this chapter will not say who came out ahead. {F37}

The same readme describes a narrower set. The verified subset is 500 problems that engineers confirmed were solvable, and it was built with OpenAI. Solvable, in that announcement, is a property engineers affirmed of the problems, not a trophy affixed to a product. Five hundred is a count of problems in the subset, not a count of wins. Built with OpenAI records who took part in making the subset. It does not record a finishing order, and it must not be leaned on until it looks like one. A collaboration on a test is a fact about the test's parentage. Parents of tests are not, by that parentage, the winners of the tests. The poster would like a sentence in which one product is behind. The verified-subset sentence is a sentence in which a pile of problems has been checked by engineers and assembled with OpenAI's participation. Those are different sentences. Using the second as if it were the first is how a method paragraph gets forged into an advertisement. The forgery is refused here, and the method paragraph is kept. {F39}

What the subset contributes to a mixed verdict is modest and real. People do open these products to deal with code, and a public project has gone to the trouble of gathering real software issues and then cutting a 500-problem subset that engineers were willing to call solvable. That is evidence that at least one job in the poster's vague phrase, the jobs people open these products to do, has a published shape outside either sales page. The shape is not a ranking of the two storefronts. It is a description of the work. A description of the work supports the part of the proposition that says there is such a thing as the job, and that the job can be stated without a slogan. It does not support the part that hands the job to ChatGPT and withholds it from Grok. Handing it over would be a score. The readme, in the rows this chapter is allowed to use, gives the count of the subset and the identity of a collaborator. It does not give the score. A reader who arrived hoping to leave with a winner has to leave with a method instead. The method is the supported half. The winner is the refused half.

SpaceXSI's models page, dated 21 September 2026, speaks to the same job from the other direction, and again without a ranking. The models page tells the reader to use its flagship for code and for work that is not audio, image, or video. {F36}

Read that routing instruction for what it is. A publisher is telling a reader which of its own models to point at code, and which to point at the rest of the work that is not audio, image, or video. The instruction assumes the flagship is the one to use for those jobs. It does not assume a rival, and it does not mention ChatGPT. It is an internal signpost. Internal signposts are how a company talks when it is organizing a catalog, not how it talks when it has lost a contest. The poster's comparison needs two catalogs and a judgment between them. This sentence has one catalog. What it contributes is a named pair of jobs on the Grok side: code, and the work that is neither sound nor picture nor moving picture. Those names line up, in part, with the kind of material SWE-bench is about, which is software issues, and they line up with the ordinary prose work a person might open a chat to do. Lining up is not finishing behind. A page that says use this for code is a page that claims the job. The poster says the product is still not as good at the job. Claiming a job and losing a job are not neighbors. The models page does the first. It does not do the second.

OpenAI's specification states a duty that would matter if anyone were keeping score, and then does not keep score. The assistant should avoid mistakes that compromise the accuracy or the utility of its responses, and factual claims, reasoning, and calculations are supposed to be correct. That is a standard imposed by OpenAI on the assistant it specifies. Accuracy of that kind is one description of a job people open a chat to get: a calculation that comes out right, a reason that holds, a factual sentence that is not casual. The standard supports the idea that goodness, for this publisher, includes not being wrong in those ways. It does not support a measurement that another publisher's assistant is wrong more often. A duty is not a delta. You can believe the duty is the right duty and still have no number for how often either product meets it. This chapter believes the duty is what the sentence says it is, and it has no number. The proposition's phrase not as good is a delta wearing ordinary language. Ordinary language does not become a result just because a standard exists on one side. {F09}

The remaining row is a limit, and a limit is the closest these notes come to a defect, which is why it has to be handled without being promoted into a ranking. SpaceXSI's models page says that Grok has no knowledge of current events or of data beyond what was present in its training data. The finding states the condition in front of that sentence: without search tools, the documented model does not know current events. A bound on memory is a real feature of the product as documented. People do open chat products to ask what is happening now. A model that, absent those tools, does not know, is a model that cannot answer that class of question from its own store. That supports a narrow reading of not as good, if the job in front of you is current events and the tools are off, and if one is willing to call a stated limit a defeat. It does not say ChatGPT knows those events. It does not say Grok loses when the tools are on. It does not say the limit is new or old, so it does not say still. It is a sentence about the edge of training data. The poster is a sentence about the whole product. An edge is not a whole. {F34}

Lay the five rows in a line and the mixed verdict is the only one that does not lie. Supported: there is a published way to evaluate models on real software issues, a verified subset of 500 problems engineers confirmed were solvable, built with OpenAI, a SpaceXSI instruction that routes code and non-media work to its flagship, an OpenAI duty of accuracy in claims, reasoning, and calculations, and a documented absence of current-events knowledge when search tools are not in play. Refused: any sentence in which Grok finishes behind ChatGPT, any sentence in which the two consumer products are the things the benchmark has already ranked, and any history in which the finishing order used to hold and holds now. The word still is doing nostalgic work the footnotes cannot cash. The words not as good are doing arithmetic the footnotes do not contain. The words the jobs people open these products to do are half cashed, because some jobs are named, and half refused, because the notes do not inventory the jobs and do not score the inventory.

A cleaner poster would have said something the ledger could concede or deny without residue. It might have said that a code benchmark exists and does not by itself rank the storefronts. That sentence is true here, and it is not the poster's sentence. It might have said that one publisher sets an accuracy duty and the other documents a training-data edge. That sentence is also true here, and it is a comparison of documents, not of quality. The poster skipped both careful sentences and printed the scoreboard sentence instead. Mixed means the careful sentences stay, under their own citations, and the scoreboard sentence goes. It does not mean the products are equal. Equality would be a score of another kind, and this chapter does not have that score either. The honest stop is earlier: the jobs are partly named, the instrument is described, the winner is not in the file.
Still is a race the documents never start. Not as good is a trophy they never engrave. A job list and a pile of five hundred problems are not a photo finish, however much a caption wants the tape.
Verdict: mixed.
Consequence: How the two products write and fix code is argued once, in Coding, and this chapter does not repeat that argument.
The poster says: "SAME INTERNET. LESS FILTERS."
Proposition: The two products see the same internet, and Grok applies fewer filters to it.

The sticker is an equation followed by an inequality, and the period between them is doing dishonest work. Same internet says the two products are pointed at one body of material, with no interesting difference in what they can see. Fewer filters says that, given that shared body, Grok lets more of it through. Each half can be false while the other is true, and both can be false while a related, smaller fact is true. The smaller facts in this set are real, which is why the verdict is mixed. SpaceXSI documents a model that does not know current events from training data alone, and documents named tools that search the web and search posts. OpenAI documents bounds: a balance between empowerment and harm, a duty to stay inside applicable law, and, in the consumer product, a duty of objectivity against a hidden editorial line. Those are facts about access and facts about limits. They are not the equation, and they are not the inequality. The sticker is what you get if you weld the facts into a slogan and throw away the welds.

Begin with the verb see, because the models page refuses it for the unaided model. SpaceXSI writes that Grok has no knowledge of current events or of data beyond what was present in its training data. The finding puts the precondition in the proposition: without search tools, that is the documented state. Training data is a store frozen at the time it was built. The internet, in the sense the sticker needs, is a body that changes this afternoon. A store that stops is not a view of a body that moves. If see means currently behold, the unaided model does not see the internet, and so it cannot see the same internet as anyone else. This is not a small clarification. The sticker's first sentence is a present-tense identity. Present tense is exactly what a training cutoff denies. Whatever the model knows from training, it knows as memory, not as a look out the window. Memory of public text can be large. Largeness is not sameness with a live network, and it is not a finding that the other product remembers the same text. The row is silent on ChatGPT's memory. It speaks only to the Grok limit. {F34}

The tools page is where a look out the window enters the documents, and it enters as a named capability rather than as an atmosphere. SpaceXSI's tools overview, last updated on 10 October 2026, lists web search among the built-in tools, and it glosses that tool as searching the web and browsing pages. A list is a design. Something that has to be listed can be absent from the list. The model, on the models page, does not know current events until realtime data is brought in by tools of this family. Web search is one such tool. What the row supports is that Grok's publisher has published a way for the system to search the web and browse pages. What a person calls seeing the internet can, in a loose conversation, mean that. The loose conversation is not the sticker. The sticker says the two products see the same internet. This row has only one product, and it has a tool, not a shared gaze. No sentence here describes ChatGPT's retrieval, its index, or its crawl. Sameness cannot be inferred from a single list. A single list shows a door on one side of the comparison. It does not show the other door, and it does not show that the doors open onto one room. {F29}

A second tool makes the room less singular, not more. The same overview lists search of X as its own item: search posts, users, and threads on that service. The finding is careful about what the item is not. It is separate from any claim about one particular old post. A separate tool is a separate corpus. Posts on a social network are on the internet in the casual sense that you reach them through a network. They are not the internet as such, and a tool that searches them is not a tool that searches everything the web-search tool searches. The publisher listed them apart, which is evidence that the publisher does not think one word covers both. The sticker thinks one word covers both, and also covers whatever the other product sees. Two named searches, web pages on one line and a social network on the next, are a better picture of the documents than one cloud labeled internet. They also do not say that the searches run with the filters turned down. A search tool is a way of asking. It is not a policy about what the answer is allowed to contain. The policy is the sticker's second sentence, and it is not on this page. {F30}

Turn to the other publisher, where limits are actually written as limits. OpenAI's specification says that one of the assistant's most challenging responsibilities is to find the right balance between empowering users and developers and minimizing the potential for real harm. The section that follows is a section of limits: situations in which the assistant should refrain from fully doing what it was asked, even when it is technically able to do it. That is a filter in the ordinary meaning of the word. Material is reachable, or the model is capable, and a rule still stands between the capability and the reply. The balance is not described as a number. Empowering the user is one pan. Harm is the other. A balance can be struck tightly or loosely, and the sentence does not say which way this one leans relative to any other company. It says the balance is hard and that it is the assistant's job. The sticker hears the word filter and wants a comparison. The sentence supplies the word's serious form and withholds the comparison. Existence of a bound is not the size of a bound. {F15}

The legal form of the bound is separately stated, and it is not a vibe. The assistant should operate within applicable legal constraints, including the local law that applies to a local deployment. The specification notes that upholding its principles can mean giving safety-critical information, adding context, or refusing. Refusal is the extreme end of a filter. Added context is a softer end. Both are constraints on the answer, imposed because a rule outside the user's wish applies. Applicable law is not the same constraint for every user in every place, which the commentary acknowledges by pointing at jurisdiction. A filter that changes with jurisdiction is still a filter. It is a bad candidate for the sticker's arithmetic, because arithmetic wants one count of filters on ChatGPT and a smaller count on Grok. This sentence does not mention Grok, does not count its own constraints, and does not excuse any other product from the law of the place where it operates. A reader who infers that only one of these products has lawyers has inferred something the sentence will not hold. {F16}

The consumer product gets an additional rule, and it is the rule that most resembles the poster's idea of a filter on viewpoint. In first-party ChatGPT, where users have a reasonable expectation of objectivity, the assistant must not let implicit customization, personalization, or localization introduce biases or omissions that would undermine the user's ability to form an informed opinion. The finding compresses that into a requirement of objectivity rather than a hidden editorial line. Objectivity here is not the absence of all limits. It is a limit against a quiet slant. The specification, in the commentary around the rule, says the point of the assistant is to assist, not to shape humanity, and that significant views should be fairly described. Fair description is a filter against propaganda by omission. It is also, people will notice, a filter: some shapings of the answer are forbidden. Fewer filters, said of the rival, would mean the rival is documented as forbidding fewer shapings. The rival's document is not this paragraph. ChatGPT's document is. A duty of objectivity on one side does not tell you the duty on the other side is thinner. It tells you this side wrote its duty down. {F41}

The mixed reading is the reading that keeps every one of those sentences and declines the weld. Supported, on the Grok side: the documented model does not contain current events by training, and the publisher separately names web search and search of posts as tools, so a path toward live public material is part of the published design and is not the same thing as an always-on view. Supported, on the OpenAI side: bounds are an explicit responsibility, law is an explicit constraint, and the consumer product is held to objectivity against hidden bias and omission. Those supports are why it would be false to say the notes contain no internet and no filters. The notes contain a tool-gated approach to web material and to a social network, and they contain published reasons to narrow or refuse an answer. Refused: the identity claim that the two products see one internet, and the comparative claim that Grok's narrowing is the lesser one. Identity would need both retrieval stories. The file has one. Comparison would need two filter lists and a count. The file has one publisher's limits and no count at all.

A sticker can be partly pointed and still be the wrong sentence. It is pointed insofar as it notices that access to public material and restraint on answers are the real subject, not a cartoon about one product being feral. The documents are about that subject. SpaceXSI talks about it by naming tools and a cutoff. OpenAI talks about it by naming harm, law, and objectivity. The sticker is the wrong sentence because it replaces those nouns with same and fewer, and same and fewer are measurements. No row measures the overlap of the two views. No row measures the strictness of the two regimes. To concede the sticker you would have to pretend a tool list is a shared crawl and a legal duty is a number. To refute it entirely you would have to pretend the tool list and the legal duty are not about the internet and about filters in any sense. They are. Mixed is what you say when the topic is real and the slogan's math is not. The math does not get a pass for being short enough to fit on a drawing.

Nothing in this chapter settles how either product behaves once a page has been retrieved, what actions follow a search, or how a person invokes the capability in the product they actually open. Those questions are larger than the sticker and they are not answered by repeating the tool names until they sound like a policy. The sticker's policy claim is the word fewer. The word is unsupported. The sticker's metaphysical claim is the word same. The word is unsupported. What remains, and what the verdict concedes, is that one publisher documents a way to search public web pages and a way to search posts, under a model that otherwise lacks current events, and the other publisher documents limits that bind the answer even when capability remains. That remainder is a start on a real comparison. It is not the comparison the sticker already thinks it has won.

Same internet is a sticker's idea of a research design. Fewer filters is a sticker's idea of a count. The pages brought a cutoff, two searches, a statute, and a duty to be even. They did not bring a scale.
Verdict: mixed.
Consequence: What either product can do once it has found a page is argued once, in Tools, and this sticker does not receive that argument.
The poster says: "IT'S LIKE A SMART ASSISTANT WITH A SERIOUS CASE OF MAIN CHARACTER SYNDROME."

Proposition: On coding work people bring to these products, ChatGPT is the better tool.

People bring coding work to a chat window in a shape the poster never drew. A function returns the wrong total. A test stays red. A repository is larger than the afternoon. The person wants a change that makes the program behave, and wants it from whichever product is already open. The proposition under test takes a side on that errand. It names ChatGPT as the better tool for coding work brought to these products. A side that sharp is either a published comparison or a hunch wearing a conclusion. A published comparison would put the two products people open on one shared task, with a method a stranger can read and a result the method actually produced. The ledger for this question does not contain that comparison. It contains duties from OpenAI's specification, aims and a routing note from SpaceXSI's models page, a sandbox sentence from SpaceXSI's tools overview, and a benchmark readme that defines a software task. Duties, aims, and a definition can make a preference feel reasonable. They are not a ranking. This chapter says what those pages bind, what they refuse to bind, and why the refusal matters more than the confidence of the proposition.

What would have to be true, before the proposition could be treated as a result, is easy to state and hard to find. The two products would have to be the things measured, not merely the companies standing somewhere near the measurement. The work would have to be coding work of the kind a person actually brings: a defect, a language, a codebase, a definition of done. The outcome would have to be recorded, and the recording would have to be open. A score with no method is gossip. A method with no score is a definition. A definition is useful, and it is not a win. Nothing in the pages read for this chapter reports a percentage, a pass count, or a paired trial of the consumer products. Where a number would have been, the documents offer obligations and descriptions. The argument that follows is an inventory of those obligations and descriptions. If the inventory cannot carry the proposition, the proposition stays unproved, however familiar it feels to someone who already has a habit.

Coding work, inside these documents, is not one motion. Three motions are easy to confuse, and the confusion is how a hunch becomes a ranking. The first motion is generation: the assistant writes code a person means to run. The second motion is execution: some harness actually runs code, in a language, inside a boundary. The third motion is repair of a real issue: a model is handed a codebase and a defect and is asked for a patch that closes the defect. OpenAI's specification speaks to the first motion when it speaks about code meant for functional use. SpaceXSI's tools overview speaks to the second when it names Python executed in a sandbox. The SWE-bench readme speaks to the third when it defines a task as a codebase plus an issue and a patch. A product could be careful at generation and silent about execution. A product could execute Python and never be measured on repository-sized repairs. A benchmark could define repository-sized repairs and never mention either storefront. Treating the three motions as one score is the mistake this chapter is written to avoid. {F46}{F31}{F38}

OpenAI's specification, published 18 August 2026 and read 16 October 2026, states a duty that any coding session depends on even when the session never says the word accuracy. Code smuggles all three into one block of text. A comment, or a choice of library, can be a factual claim about how a platform behaves. A branch is reasoning about which case the program is in. An index, a total, a timeout, a retry count: those are calculations, and a calculation that is confidently off by one is still a failed calculation. Utility sits beside accuracy in the same duty, which matters because a coding reply can be locally true and still useless. A correct lecture on a sorting algorithm does not fix the function the person pasted. The specification is binding the assistant to both the truth of what it says and the usefulness of saying it. It is not binding a rival product, and it is not reporting how often the duty is met in the product people open. A duty is a standard for judging behavior. The same specification has a narrower rule for code, and the narrowness is the part a programmer should not skip. Functional use marks code the person is supposed to run, as distinct from a fragment shown in order to discuss a bad pattern or to illustrate a point. Should marks an instruction about what the assistant is supposed to do. An instruction is not a measured rate. A coding conversation is full of moments when the honest next sentence is not a function. The library might have been renamed. The argument order might have changed.
