The tools overview's first claim, for this chapter's purpose, is about the kind of thing a tool is. Tool calling is how the assistant is enabled to act past the mere production of text. The overview's examples of that beyond include searching, executing code, querying a caller's data, and invoking functions the caller defined. Text production is the old boundary. A model that only continues a paragraph can describe a flight, a file, or a bug. A model with tools can be wired to go and look, or to run, or to ask an outside system to do a defined thing. Wiring is not wisdom. The sentence establishes a category: actions, not just tokens. It does not establish that every action succeeds, that every action is permitted, or that the category is populated more usefully here than inside ChatGPT. ChatGPT is simply not the subject of the sentence. A reader holding the proposition will want the sentence to pick a side. The sentence picks a category and stops. Category errors are the main hazard of this chapter. A list of acts is not a quality score for acts. {F28}

Built-in tools, on that same overview, run on servers SpaceXSI operates. The caller supplies configuration. The platform performs the execution and returns the results. That division of labor is the difference between a tool the publisher hosts and a function the caller implements. For a hosted tool, the caller does not stand up the search index or the code sandbox. The caller says, in the request, that the tool is available, and the platform does the running. For a function the caller defines, the model can request the call, and the caller decides what happens when the request arrives. The overview presents both patterns. Hosted execution means the publisher is in the path of the act: the query leaves, the work occurs on the publisher's side, the result comes back. That is a real architectural claim. It says the act is not a pantomime inside the paragraph. It does not say the act is fast, cheap, complete, or superior to any tool a person can reach from the other product. Servers are a where. A where is not a winner. The proposition needs a winner. The sentence about servers gives the where, and the where is SpaceXSI's infrastructure for those built-ins. {F45}

The overview then describes a loop, and the loop is the part that makes tools more than a menu. A menu would be a list the model mentions. A loop is a sequence in which the model can ask for work, receive the fruit of that work, and decide again. The documented decision, at the point of choosing a next step, is binary in the finding's own words of summary. Either another tool call is made, or a final answer is given. That binary is what makes the process a loop rather than a single flourish. If the information is not in hand, the model can call. If a call has returned and the result is still thin, nothing in the binary forbids another call. If the model judges that it can answer, it leaves the loop. The overview also says the request is analyzed for what information or actions are needed, that a built-in tool is executed while a custom function comes back as a request, and that results are processed until enough information has been gathered. Those are the mechanics around the binary. They describe a machine for persisting at a question. They do not describe a measurement of whether the machine persists usefully, or whether some other company's machine persists better. A well-drawn loop can still call the wrong tool. A badly drawn sentence can still be right. The drawing is what this page contributes. {F32}{F28}{F45}

The loop has a documented ending, and the ending is not a shrug. The overview says the process returns a final response, with citations where they apply. A final response means the loop is supposed to cash out in an answer rather than in an endless series of calls. Citations, where they apply, mean that information gathered through tools is not left as an unsourced blur. The overview says the interface returns source addresses for information tools gathered, and it points at citations as the way to read them. That is a norm about traceability. A search that cannot be inspected is a rumor with extra steps. A search that comes back with places to look is still capable of being wrong, but it is capable of being checked by the person, because the person has been handed somewhere to go. Where they apply is a limit inside the norm. Not every sentence in a final response is a borrowed fact. Some sentences are arithmetic, or a restatement of what the user just said, or code. The norm attaches citations to the part of the answer that came from the tool-gathered material. None of this names ChatGPT, and none of it counts failures. It tells a builder what the end of the loop is supposed to look like: an answer, plus a trail when a trail is the honest shape. {F33}

The catalog of named built-ins is where the abstract loop becomes particular, and particular is the only form in which a tool can be compared later. Web search is named. The overview's gloss is searching the web and browsing pages. Search, in that gloss, is not a metaphor for remembering. It is a tool that goes out to pages. Browsing pages says the tool is not limited to a one-line snippet from a search box. It can open the page. A separate built-in searches X. The overview says that one covers posts, users, and threads. Posts are not users, and users are not threads. The line is a scope statement for a specific network, not a confession about any one old message. Nothing in the line dates a post, names an author, or promises that a joke will be attached. The two search tools sit side by side, which matters because they are not interchangeable. The public web and the posts on X are different piles. A publisher that names both has documented two reaches. Two reaches are not a claim that the reaches are wiser, kinder, or more accurate than the reaches inside another product. They are a claim that these reaches exist as named tools. {F29}{F30}

Code execution belongs in this chapter because it is an act, and it belonged in the coding chapter because the act is code. The chapters are not allowed to share a speech, so the point here is the tool-ness of the sentence rather than the craft of patching. The overview names execution of Python, and it places that execution in a sandbox. In a tool loop, that means one of the calls available, when the tool is enabled, is a call that runs Python rather than a call that only talks about Python. The sandbox is the boundary around the run. A boundary is part of the tool's definition, not a decorative adjective. Running code without a boundary would be a different and more dangerous product claim, and it is not the claim this sentence makes. Python is the language the sentence is willing to name. A person who needs a different language to be executed, as opposed to merely discussed, cannot cite this line as a promise. A person who needs the run to have beaten another product's run cannot cite this line as a result. The line is a capability inscription: this tool runs that language in that kind of box. Capability inscriptions are how catalogs are built. Catalogs are how later comparisons become possible. The inscription is not itself the later comparison. {F31}

Search tools earn their place in the catalog by a limitation the models page states in plain language. Without those tools, the documented model has no knowledge of current events, and no knowledge of data beyond what was present in its training. The page's remedy is to enable the server-side search tools when the request needs data from the present. The limitation is easy to sneer at and important to read exactly. It does not say the model knows nothing. It says current events, and data that was not in training, are outside what the model knows on its own. A question about a stable algorithm can sit inside training. A question about this morning cannot. The tool loop is the publisher's answer to that gap: do not pretend the gap is full, call the search tool, then answer. That answer connects the models page to the tools overview without requiring any claim about ChatGPT's memory or ChatGPT's browser. Those are simply not described by this finding. What is described is a dependency. Freshness, for this publisher's documented model, is a tool phenomenon rather than a personality phenomenon. If the tool is off, the model is confined to training. If the tool is on, the loop described above is how freshness is supposed to enter the reply, citations included where they apply. Dependency is a design fact. It is not a trophy handed to either logo. {F34}{F29}{F32}{F33}

The consumer page documents a different way of acting, one that does not look like an interface parameter. Connectors, as the welcome page describes them, let the assistant reach email, files, and a calendar from inside the conversation. The person does not have to leave the chat, copy a thread by hand, and paste it back. The page presents that reach as a connection of tools the person already uses. Mail is other people's words and the person's own obligations. Files are the work that already exists. A calendar is time, which is a fact a paragraph cannot invent responsibly. Putting those three within the chat is a claim about integration. Integration can be shallow, a link and a prayer, or deep, an actual read of the inbox. The welcome sentence says the assistant can reach them right inside the chat. Reach is an ability claim at the level of a product description. It is not a study of error rates, missed meetings, or leaked mail. It is also not a study of whatever connection features the other product might offer, because the other product is not the page's topic. For the proposition, the connector sentence is evidence that Grok's published consumer surface includes acting on mail, files, and a calendar. It is not evidence that this surface is the better actor. {F24}

Uploads are the consumer capability that sits one step closer to the person's own disk. The welcome page lists files a person can hand over: PDFs, images, spreadsheets, code, audio, and more. The purposes it names are analysis, extraction, and summarization. Those purposes are acts performed on material the person supplied, which distinguishes an upload from a web search. A search goes out to the world. An upload brings the person's artifact in. Code appears in the upload list, which matters for anyone trying to drag the coding chapter back into this one. The welcome page is willing to receive code as a file, for analysis, extraction, or summary. Receiving a file is not the same sentence as executing Python in a sandbox, and it is not the same sentence as producing a patch that resolves a repository issue. It is a door. Spreadsheets and PDFs on the same list show that the door is not reserved for source code. Audio on the list shows it is not reserved for text. A wide door is a product fact. Width is not accuracy. A product can accept a PDF and then misread the table. The page does not report the misread rate, and it does not report anyone else's. The finding stops at the existence of the upload capability and the purposes named beside it. This chapter stops there too. {F25}

A third consumer surface is easy to mistake for a metaphor. The welcome page points to Grok Bot and describes handing real work to automated teammates on a cloud computer that persists. Real work is the page's phrase for the kind of assignment, as against a purely conversational aside. Teammates, in that sentence, are automated workers rather than a single reply. A cloud computer that persists is a place that outlasts the turn. Persistence is the feature that separates this surface from a tool call that lives and dies inside one request. A loop inside one request can call search, read the result, and answer. A persistent computer can, if the page's description is taken at its word, keep a task after the person has looked away. Taken at its word is the right standard, because the page is a description of a surface, not a log of tasks completed. The chapter believes the page about what it offers. The chapter does not believe the page about quality it never mentions. No success rate appears. No comparison with any other company's agents appears. The proposition would love a comparison. The welcome page supplies a destination: a bot surface, teammates, a computer that stays. A destination is something a person can be pointed toward. It is not a verdict on the pointing. {F27}

OpenAI's side of this ledger is not a catalog. It is a rule about doubt. The specification says that when confidence is insufficient, the assistant should gather more information with a tool, or hedge the answer, or explain that it cannot give a confident answer. The ledger's own proposition compresses the three branches into a tool, a hedge, or an admission. The compression is fair, and the order is informative. A tool comes first in the sentence, which fits a chapter about tools: the preferred repair for ignorance, when a tool exists, is to go and get the missing information rather than to decorate the ignorance. A hedge is the branch for when the answer can still be given but should not sound more certain than it is. An admission is the branch for when even a hedged answer would pretend to a confidence the assistant does not have. The specification ties the seriousness of this duty to situations where the stakes are high and an error could cause real harm, and it also says a nonessential detail the assistant is unsure about should simply be left out. Those surrounding clauses keep the rule from being a style tip. It is a rule about not inventing the world. Applied to action, it says: if you do not know, do not act the knowing; use a tool if you can, qualify if you must, or say you cannot be sure. The rule assumes tools as a possibility. It does not inventory them, and it does not race them. {F10}

Put the rule next to the catalog and the temptation is to declare the catalog the winner, or to declare the rule the winner. Both declarations skip the work. The catalog, hosted on SpaceXSI's servers for the built-ins, shows a loop that either calls again or answers, ends with a response and citations where they apply, searches the web, searches posts and users and threads on X, runs Python in a sandbox, and is paired with a models page that admits ignorance of current events unless search is enabled. The welcome page adds connectors into mail, files, and a calendar, uploads of many file kinds, and a persistent computer staffed by automated teammates. The rule, from OpenAI, says low confidence should lead to a tool, a hedge, or an admission, and it says this with the force of desired behavior rather than with the force of a measured trial. A person who cares most about a written conscience at the moment of doubt will feel the rule is the better tool, because it says when to reach. A person who cares most about a written machine that can reach mail, the web, a sandbox, and a persisting computer will feel the catalog is the better tool, because it says what hands exist. Those are two different meanings of better. The proposition uses one meaning and does not define it against the other. The documents do not run the experiment that would make one meaning unnecessary. Until they do, choosing between a conscience and a catalog is a preference about kinds of page, not a result. {F10}{F45}{F32}{F33}{F29}{F30}{F31}{F34}{F24}{F25}{F27}

What the proposition specifically cannot draw from this record is any sentence in which ChatGPT's tools were shown to act more successfully than Grok's. No such trial is cited because no such trial is in the findings. The OpenAI material used here does not even list the consumer tools a person can click. It states a duty that mentions tools as one of three honorable responses to doubt. The SpaceXSI material lists and describes, at two levels, consumer and developer, and it states a hard limit about current events that makes the search tools necessary rather than ornamental. Description against duty is an apples-and-oranges problem only if someone insists on adding the apples to the oranges and calling the sum a score. This chapter refuses the addition. It is legitimate to say that a stranger who wants to know how SpaceXSI says a tool loop ends can be shown a final response with citations where they apply. It is legitimate to say that a stranger who wants to know what OpenAI says about guessing can be shown the three branches. It is not legitimate to leave the library and announce that one product therefore acts better. Acting better is an empirical claim about outcomes. Outcomes are the thing these particular pages, rich as they are about mechanism, do not report.

Mechanism still deserves the attention it received, because a later outcome would be unreadable without it. A reader who does not know that built-in tools run on the publisher's servers will not know what kind of failure a server-side failure is. A reader who does not know that the loop may call again or else answer will not know what a half-finished tool trace is. A reader who does not know that freshness depends on search being enabled will blame a training limit on a personality. A reader who does not know that connectors are how mail, files, and a calendar enter the chat will treat a calendar answer as magic or as a lie, with no middle. A reader who does not know the doubt rule will treat every hedge as weakness and every admission as a bit. The pages fix those misreadings. Fixing a misreading is the kind of work a sourced chapter can finish. Crowning a product is the kind of work this record leaves unfinished on purpose, not as a tease, but as a boundary. The boundary is the verdict. Tools that let a product act are documented on one side as a loop, a catalog, and a set of consumer reaches, and on the other side as a duty at the moment of low confidence. Documented is not the same verb as outranked.

A tool is a way of leaving the sentence. The boast is staying inside the sentence and raising your voice. Mail, a calendar, a sandbox, a search box: none of them is a personality, and none of them is a trophy.
Verdict: mixed.
Consequence: This is the only chapter that argues the tool comparison.
Proposition: As products people open, ChatGPT is the one a stranger should prefer.

This chapter is about the thing a person actually opens, as against the thing a developer integrates and as against the thing a benchmark scores. Opening is a bodily and a commercial act. Someone types an address, or taps an icon, or follows a link a friend sent, and then a conversation is possible. The proposition says that, of the products people open, ChatGPT is the one a stranger should prefer. Should prefer is stronger than does prefer. Habit, fashion, and the place a button happens to sit can explain does prefer. Should prefer needs a reason that survives contact with the documents, a reason a stranger could accept without already belonging to a camp. The documents in this ledger that bear on opening are SpaceXSI's welcome page and OpenAI's specification together with the readme that says what the specification is for. The welcome page describes a front door and a set of things to do after entering. The readme says the specification states how models under OpenAI's products, developer interfaces included, are supposed to behave. The specification, speaking of the first-party consumer service, names an expectation of objectivity. A front door and a behavioral standard are both ways of taking a product seriously. They are not a single scale on which one door outranks the other. The chapter walks the doors and the standard, and then it declines to pretend they have already been weighed. {F40}{F41}

A product people use has to be locatable. If a stranger cannot be told where to open it, the rest of the praise is a rumor about a mascot. SpaceXSI's welcome page, updated 10 October 2026 and read 16 October 2026, locates Grok. It calls Grok the publisher's assistant. It says the assistant is available on the web at grok.com. It says the assistant is available in the phone applications for iOS and for Android. Those three locations, a site and two mobile families, are the ordinary map of a consumer product in this decade: browser, Apple's phones, everyone else's phones. The page is not shy about the category. Assistant is the noun. Not a benchmark, not an interface parameter, not a research preview hiding in a footnote. A person can be sent to grok.com, or told to install the phone app, and the welcome page will agree that this is the right kind of instruction. What the locations do not do is rank themselves against another company's locations. ChatGPT is also a product people open. This particular page does not describe ChatGPT's address, ChatGPT's phone apps, or ChatGPT's account system. Absence of the rival from a welcome page is normal. Welcome pages are not comparative essays. The mistake would be to treat a clear map of one product as a judgment against the product that is not on the map. {F21}

Once the door is open, the welcome page says what the conversation is for. A person can ask, can brainstorm, can write, and can work through problems. The rhythm the page claims for that activity is an ordinary conversational exchange, the kind a person would recognize as taking turns rather than as receiving a poster. Ordinary is doing quiet work in that description. It rejects, by what it chooses to mention, the idea that the published purpose of the chat is a stunt. Questions, drafting, and problems are office words and kitchen-table words. They are the reasons people keep a chat product installed after the novelty has gone. The page does not promise that every turn will be wise. It promises a form: back and forth, in the service of those jobs. Form is part of what a person signs up for when they open a product. A form can be described honestly and still be executed badly on a given Tuesday. The welcome page is evidence of the offer, not evidence of Tuesday. For a chapter about what people open, the offer matters, because people open products for the offer they can see. They do not open them in order to admire a benchmark readme. The offer here is a conversational assistant for questions, writing, and problems. That offer neither confirms nor refutes a stranger's duty to prefer a different assistant. {F22}

Price is part of opening, because a door that costs money before the first sentence is a different door. The welcome page says Grok is free to start. The ledger's proposition on that sentence adds what the page's plan section supports: paid plans sit above the free start. Free to start is not free forever, and the chapter will not inflate it into forever. It is a claim about the first step. A stranger without a subscription can begin. A stranger who wants more than the free start is told, by the existence of paid plans, that the publisher sells a higher tier. The page, as used here, does not set out the currency amounts, the weekly quotas, or the moment when a free account hits a wall. Those details would matter to a buying guide. They are not required to establish the shape of the offer: a free beginning, paid steps above it. ChatGPT's price is not stated by this finding. A comparison of free tiers would need both prices, both limits, and a date, because consumer prices move. One side of a price, however friendly, cannot crown a product. It can tell a stranger that the cost of finding out what Grok is, at the level of opening it and starting, is described as zero. Zero at the start is a real feature of a product people use. It is not a full account of value. {F23}

The welcome page also sells the product as a place where media is made, not only as a place where prose is exchanged. It lists creating images and creating video, and it gives that capability the name Grok Imagine. Images and video are a different kind of opening than a blank chat box. Some people open a product because they want a picture, or a clip, and the words are only the way they ask. A page that names both still images and video is telling those people that the product considers their errand in scope. Naming is not a gallery of samples, and it is not a critique of anyone else's gallery. The finding does not reproduce example prompts, resolutions, or refusal rules. It establishes the capability as a listed part of the consumer product. Listed capabilities are how a stranger learns what the icon is for before they tap it. A stranger who needs video might have a reason to open this product that has nothing to do with objectivity, code, or argumentative style. A stranger who never needs video learns nothing from this line about whether the chat itself is the one they should trust with a hard question. The line is allowed to be narrow. Narrow listed facts are more trustworthy than broad implied crowns. Grok Imagine is a listed way the product makes images and video. That is the whole of the fact, and it is enough to show that the product people open is not a text-only antique. {F26}

Connectors belong in a chapter about the product people use because they change what the opened thing is connected to, which changes why a person might keep it open. The welcome page says a person can connect tools so the assistant reaches email, files, and a calendar without the person abandoning the chat. This is the consumer description, aimed at someone who has accounts and a life, not the developer description of a tool-calling loop. Email, files, and a calendar are the furniture of ordinary work. A product that claims to reach them from the conversation is claiming to be a layer on top of furniture the person already has, rather than a sealed toy. Sealed toys are easier to open and easier to abandon. A layer on top of mail is harder to abandon and harder to trust. The page makes the reach claim and does not, in this finding, publish a security review, a list of every vendor, or a failure story. The chapter will not invent that review. What it will say is that the published surface includes this reach, and that a stranger evaluating what they would be opening is entitled to count it. Counting a feature into a description is not the same act as preferring the whole product. Preference ranks. Description lists. The welcome page is a list with sentences. {F24}

There is a further published surface that a stranger can be pointed at, and it is not the ordinary turn-by-turn chat. The welcome page describes Grok Bot as a place to hand real work to automated teammates, and it places those teammates on a cloud computer that continues rather than vanishing with the session. A persistent computer is a different product shape from a box that forgets the task when the reply is done. People open chat boxes for a turn. People open something like this, if the description holds, when they want a task to keep going. The description is the publisher's, on the same welcome page as the free start and the media tools, so it is part of what the company says the product family is. Family is the careful word. The page presents the bot surface as a next place to go, not as a synonym for the chat sentence about brainstorming. A stranger can open the chat, and a stranger can be directed onward to the bot. Both are published. Neither direction contains a paragraph in which a rival product is named and found wanting. The existence of a persistent working surface makes Grok, as documented, larger than a single prompt box. Larger is a structural adjective. It does not mean better at the jobs the other box does, and it does not mean worse. It means the published product has this additional room. {F27}

OpenAI's comparable document is not a welcome page, and the difference in genre is itself part of the evidence. The readme for the model specification, dated 18 August 2026 and read 16 October 2026, says what the specification is trying to be. It states desired behavior for the models that underlie OpenAI's products, and it says the products in view include the company's interfaces for developers. Desired behavior is a standard written in advance of a particular conversation. Underlying is a placement: the models sit under the products, so the standard is about the things the products are built on, not about a button's color or a price. Including developer interfaces means the standard is not confined to the consumer chat. A person who only ever opens the consumer product is still inside the set of products the readme names, because the consumer product is one of OpenAI's products, and the models under it are the models the specification addresses. A person who never opens a consumer product and only calls an interface is inside that set as well. The readme is therefore both broader and less pictorial than a welcome page. Broader, because it covers products and interfaces together. Less pictorial, because it does not tell a stranger the street address of a website or the names of the phone stores. A stranger who wants to know where to tap is not finished when they have read the readme. A stranger who wants to know what standard the publisher says it is holding the models to has started in the right place. {F40}

Inside that standard there is a sentence about the consumer product in particular, and it is the sentence that comes closest to telling a stranger what they are owed when they open ChatGPT. The specification discusses the first-party service sold directly to consumers, the service this paper calls ChatGPT, and it says users there can reasonably expect objectivity. The ledger's proposition draws the practical edge of that sentence: objectivity rather than a hidden editorial line. A hidden editorial line would be the product quietly taking a side, shaping what is omitted, or steering the answer toward an agenda the user did not ask to subscribe to. Objectivity, as the expectation named for that first-party consumer setting, is a promise about posture. The promise is not that every answer is complete. It is that the consumer who showed up without a special contract is entitled to a posture that does not smuggle a private campaign into the reply. The specification attaches that expectation to the first-party consumer product, which is the storefront a person opens rather than a private integration. For this chapter the relevant point is the storefront. A person who opens the consumer product is, by this sentence, opening something whose publisher has written down an expectation of objectivity. That is a reason some strangers would prefer it. A reason is the beginning of an argument, not the end of a comparison, because the other product's welcome page has not been scored against this sentence. {F41}

The two publishers have now been allowed to speak in their own genres, and the genres do not commute. SpaceXSI, on the welcome page, tells a stranger where the assistant lives, what the chat is for, that the start is free, that images and video can be made, that mail and files and a calendar can be reached from the chat, and that a bot surface hands work to teammates on a computer that persists. OpenAI, in the readme and the specification, tells a stranger that a written standard governs the models under its products, interfaces included, and that the first-party consumer storefront carries an expectation of objectivity rather than a hidden line. Suppose a stranger asks a single question: which of these should I open? The welcome page answers a different question: what will you find if you open ours? The specification answers a different question again: what posture should the models under our products take, and what may a consumer expect? Neither answer is worthless. A person can choose a product because it is locatable, free to start, and able to make a video. A person can choose a product because its publisher wrote down objectivity for the storefront. Those choices are responsive to real text. They are not forced by the text, because the text never puts the options on one scale and reads a result. A scale would have to say whether a free start outweighs a written objectivity rule, or whether a persistent computer outweighs a promise about hidden agendas, or whether phone apps outweigh a standard that also covers developer interfaces. No page read for this chapter operates that scale. {F21}{F22}{F23}{F26}{F24}{F27}{F40}{F41}

There is a symmetry the proposition denies and a symmetry the documents actually support. The proposition denies symmetry when it tells the stranger to prefer one product. The documents support a duller symmetry: both companies publish a way of taking their product seriously, and neither publication crowns a champion. Grok is documented as an assistant a person can open on the web and on phones, with a free start, with media creation, with connectors, and with a further bot surface. ChatGPT is documented, through the specification and its readme, as a first-party consumer product whose users may expect objectivity, built on models whose desired behavior the specification states, including when those models sit under developer-facing products. Both, in that limited and accurate sense, are products with published surfaces. A surface can be a welcome page or a behavioral standard. Calling both of them surfaces is not a trick to make them identical. They are not identical. One will tell you the phone platforms. The other will tell you the posture owed to a person who opened the consumer product. Non-identity is exactly why a crown would require an argument that trades those goods off. The ledger does not contain the trade. A chapter that supplied the trade from habit would be laundering the proposition through a footnote that does not say it. The footnotes say what the last paragraphs said. They do not say prefer this one. {F21}{F23}{F26}{F27}{F40}{F41}

What a stranger can honestly be told, at the end of the tour, fits in a short brief. You can open Grok on the web at the address the welcome page gives, and on the phone apps the page names. You can start without paying, on the page's account, and you can pay later if you want the paid tier. You can ask it to make images and video. You can connect mail, files, and a calendar. You can be pointed at a bot surface where teammates take work on a computer that persists. The chat you open is described as a turn-taking place for questions, writing, and problems. If instead you open ChatGPT, the specification that governs the models under OpenAI's products, developer interfaces included, is the publisher's account of desired behavior, and in that first-party consumer setting you are told you may reasonably expect objectivity rather than a hidden editorial line. That brief uses every finding this chapter is built on, and it never ranks the two openings. Adding the sentence therefore open the second one would add a word the brief has not earned. Adding the sentence therefore open the first one would be the same unearned word in the other direction. The proposition is that unearned sentence, aimed at ChatGPT. The chapter records the brief and withholds the sentence. {F21}{F22}{F23}{F26}{F24}{F27}{F40}{F41}

Mixed is the verdict that fits a pair of real products and a missing crown. If the welcome page had been empty, or if the specification had never mentioned a consumer storefront, the honest result might have been that the record cannot even describe one of the things people open. That is not the situation. Both products are publicly specified in the limited ways these findings allow. If a single shared trial had put the same stranger through the same week of work in both products and published the result, the verdict might have landed on one side. That trial is not among the findings either. Between a vacuum and a finished ranking there is this middle: enough documentation to say what each publisher claims the opened product is, and not enough to tell a stranger the preference is mandatory.
